items.prompt: What is a "timeout" in this unit's sense?
choices: A maximum duration a call to a dependency is allowed to take before it's treated as failed
The total lifetime of a server process before it's automatically restarted
A delay intentionally added before a request is sent
The maximum number of requests a service can handle per second
items.explanation: A timeout is specifically about capping how long a single call is allowed to take — not a process lifetime, an intentional delay, or a rate limit.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what happened to requests waiting on the slow inventory call because there was no timeout?
choices: They held a connection indefinitely, eventually exhausting the order service's own connection pool
They were automatically canceled after 10 seconds by the operating system
They were queued in a separate, unlimited backup pool with no effect on other requests
They immediately failed and returned an error to the user
items.explanation: Without a timeout, the Scenario's requests held connections indefinitely — that resource exhaustion is exactly what caused the cascading outage.

items.prompt: What is "retry with backoff"?
choices: Automatically re-attempting a failed call, typically waiting progressively longer between attempts
Reverting a deployment to the previous version after a failure
Automatically restarting a crashed server process
A technique for compressing network traffic between services
items.explanation: Retry with backoff is specifically about re-attempting a failed call with increasing delays — not deployment rollback, process restart, or compression.

items.prompt: Why does retry logic typically use backoff (increasing delay) rather than immediately retrying?
choices: Immediately re-attempting with no delay can add more load to an already-struggling dependency right when it's least able to handle it
Backoff is required by most programming language specifications
Backoff makes the retry logic run faster overall
There's no real reason — backoff is just a stylistic convention with no functional purpose
items.explanation: L2 explicitly ties backoff to avoiding additional load on a struggling dependency — not a language requirement or a speed optimization.

items.prompt: What is a "circuit breaker" in this unit's sense?
choices: A mechanism that stops sending requests to a dependency after it fails repeatedly, then periodically checks if it has recovered
A physical hardware component that cuts power to a server rack
A code review process for changes to critical infrastructure
A rate limiter that caps how many requests a client can send per minute
items.explanation: In this unit's context, a circuit breaker is a software pattern for stopping calls to a failing dependency — not a hardware component, review process, or rate limiter.

items.prompt: Does a circuit breaker permanently stop calling a dependency once it detects failures?
choices: No — after a cooldown period, it allows a trial request through to check whether the dependency has recovered
Yes — once opened, a circuit breaker never allows any further requests to that dependency
No, but only if a human manually resets it
Yes, unless the entire service is redeployed
items.explanation: A circuit breaker is designed to periodically re-test the dependency via a trial request after a cooldown, not to block it forever or require manual/redeploy intervention.

items.prompt: What is "backpressure"?
choices: A signal sent upstream indicating a system can't keep up with the current load, so the sender can slow down or shed work
The physical pressure inside a server's cooling system
A metric tracking how much disk space a service has used
A technique for compressing HTTP responses before sending them
items.explanation: Backpressure is specifically an upstream overload signal — not a physical/hardware metric, disk usage, or compression technique.

items.prompt: Per L1, what's the alternative to backpressure that L1 contrasts it with?
choices: Silently queuing all incoming work until the system runs out of resources
Immediately rejecting every single incoming request with no exceptions
Automatically scaling up infrastructure with no upper limit
Randomly dropping a fixed percentage of requests regardless of load
items.explanation: L1 explicitly contrasts backpressure with silently queuing everything until collapse — not blanket rejection, unlimited autoscaling, or random dropping.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, did the order service's own code have a bug?
choices: No — the Scenario explicitly states the order service's own code has no bug
Yes — the order service had a memory leak unrelated to the inventory call
Yes — the order service's checkout logic contained an off-by-one error
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's facts whether there was a bug
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that the order service's own code has no bug — the outage came entirely from an unprotected dependency call.

items.prompt: Why did the order service become unable to serve requests that never touched inventory at all?
choices: Its finite connection pool was entirely filled with requests stuck waiting on the slow inventory call, leaving none free for any other request
The inventory service directly crashed the order service's process
A load balancer misconfiguration routed all traffic to inventory instead of order
The order service was manually taken offline for scheduled maintenance
items.explanation: The mechanism is pool exhaustion — stuck inventory-bound requests consumed every available connection, starving unrelated requests of resources.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, would a timeout alone have fully solved the Scenario's outage?
choices: Only partially — it frees each stuck connection sooner, but without a circuit breaker the service keeps sending new requests to the still-slow dependency
Yes — a timeout alone is described as a complete fix for any dependency degradation
No — a timeout provides no benefit at all in the Scenario
Yes, but only if the timeout value is set to exactly zero
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames a timeout as a partial fix — it bounds each wasted call, but doesn't stop new wasted calls from continuing to be made.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does a circuit breaker protect that a timeout alone doesn't?
choices: It protects the caller's resources (and the struggling dependency) from continuing to attempt calls that are very likely to fail
It protects against network packet corruption during transmission
It protects against SQL injection attacks on the dependency's database
It protects against the caller's code containing a syntax error
items.explanation: L2 attributes this specific protection to circuit breakers — stopping wasted attempts — not security, syntax, or transmission-layer concerns.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what happens to a request when the circuit breaker is in the "open" state?
choices: The call fails immediately with no network attempt at all, freeing the caller's resources instantly
The request is queued indefinitely until the breaker closes again
The request is automatically routed to a backup dependency
The request proceeds normally, exactly as if the breaker were closed
items.explanation: L2's diagram specifies that open-state calls fail instantly without attempting the network call — not queuing, backup routing, or normal proceeding.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what happens in the "half-open" state?
choices: Exactly one trial request is allowed through to test whether the dependency has recovered
All requests are allowed through simultaneously to fully re-test the dependency
The breaker permanently transitions to closed regardless of outcome
The breaker immediately reopens without allowing any requests
items.explanation: L2's diagram specifies a single trial request in half-open, not a full flood of requests or an automatic, outcome-independent transition.

items.prompt: Per L2, why not just retry forever until a failing dependency comes back?
choices: Retrying forever against a still-down dependency keeps consuming the caller's own resources on calls very likely to fail — the same resource-exhaustion problem as the Scenario
Retrying forever is technically impossible in most programming languages
There's no downside — L2 recommends retrying forever as the best practice
Retrying forever is illegal under most companies' engineering policies
items.explanation: L2 explicitly ties infinite retries to the same resource-exhaustion failure mode the Scenario already illustrated — just caused by retry logic instead of a single hanging call.

items.prompt: Per L2, is a circuit breaker meant to replace retry logic entirely?
choices: No — they address different parts of the problem, and L2 presents them as complementary techniques, not substitutes for each other
Yes — L2 states circuit breakers make retry logic entirely unnecessary
Yes, but only for dependencies with sub-second expected latency
No, but only because most languages don't support implementing circuit breakers
items.explanation: L2's table presents all four techniques as solving different parts of the same problem, not as interchangeable or mutually exclusive.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with setting a timeout much longer than a dependency's actual expected latency?
choices: A generously long timeout still lets a flood of slow requests exhaust the connection pool, just more slowly than with no timeout at all
There's no real issue — any timeout value, however long, fully solves resource exhaustion
A long timeout only matters for dependencies handling financial transactions
A long timeout causes the caller's code to fail to compile
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns that an overly generous timeout still permits pool exhaustion, just at a slower rate — the value has to match actual expected latency.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of retrying without backoff?
choices: Immediately re-attempting with no delay can add more load to an already-struggling dependency right when it's least able to handle it
There's no risk — retrying without backoff is described as strictly better than retrying with backoff
The only risk is slightly higher CPU usage on the caller, with no effect on the dependency
This risk only applies to dependencies running on cloud infrastructure specifically
items.explanation: L2 ties the risk directly to worsening the dependency's own struggling state by adding immediate, repeated load.

items.prompt: Fix CircuitBreaker's recordFailure and canAttempt so it opens after reaching the failure threshold and blocks further attempts while open.

tests.description: opens after reaching the failure threshold
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 2, cooldownMs: 1000 }); b.recordFailure(); b.recordFailure(); return b.state; })()).toBe("open")

tests.description: blocks further attempts while open and cooldown hasn't elapsed
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 2, cooldownMs: 1000 }); b.recordFailure(); b.recordFailure(); return b.canAttempt(); })()).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Counting consecutive failures and opening once the threshold is reached is what stops further wasted attempts — checking canAttempt() before every call, and having it return false while open and within the cooldown, is what actually prevents new calls from being made to a dependency that's very likely to fail.
items.reference:
🔒 Closed — requests flow, failures are counted
🚫 Open — calls fail instantly, no network attempt

Why: failing fast while open is what protects the caller's own resources from being spent on doomed requests.

items.prompt: Fix CircuitBreaker's recordFailure and canAttempt so it opens after reaching the failure threshold and blocks further attempts while open.

tests.description: opens after reaching a threshold of 3 failures
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 3, cooldownMs: 2000 }); b.recordFailure(); b.recordFailure(); b.recordFailure(); return b.state; })()).toBe("open")

tests.description: does not open before reaching the threshold
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 3, cooldownMs: 2000 }); b.recordFailure(); b.recordFailure(); return b.state; })()).toBe("closed")

items.explanation: Same fix regardless of the threshold value: counting consecutive failures and transitioning to open once the threshold is met, checked before every call via canAttempt(), is what stops further wasted attempts.
items.reference:
🔒 Closed — requests flow, failures are counted
🚫 Open — calls fail instantly, no network attempt

Why: failing fast while open is what protects the caller's own resources from being spent on doomed requests.

items.prompt: Fix CircuitBreaker's canAttempt so that once the cooldown has elapsed, it transitions to "half-open" and allows a trial request, and fix recordSuccess so a successful trial closes the breaker again.

tests.description: with a zero-length cooldown, an open breaker immediately allows a trial and moves to half-open
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 1, cooldownMs: 0 }); b.recordFailure(); const allowed = b.canAttempt(); return allowed && b.state === "half-open"; })()).toBe(true)

tests.description: a successful trial in half-open closes the breaker
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 1, cooldownMs: 0 }); b.recordFailure(); b.canAttempt(); b.recordSuccess(); return b.state; })()).toBe("closed")

tests.description: recordSuccess resets the consecutive failure count
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 3, cooldownMs: 0 }); b.recordFailure(); b.recordFailure(); b.recordSuccess(); return b.consecutiveFailures; })()).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Checking the elapsed cooldown inside canAttempt() is what lets the breaker test recovery instead of staying open forever, and resetting the failure count on success is what lets a healthy dependency fully return to normal, unthrottled traffic.
items.reference:
🕒 Half-open — one trial request allowed after the cooldown
✅ Success — resets failures and returns to closed
❌ Failure — reopens the breaker, cooldown starts again

Why: a breaker that never re-tests a recovered dependency leaves it permanently, needlessly blocked — but a still-broken dependency should reopen it immediately.

items.prompt: Fix CircuitBreaker's canAttempt so that once the cooldown has elapsed, it transitions to "half-open" and allows a trial request, and fix recordFailure so a failed trial in half-open reopens the breaker.

tests.description: with a zero-length cooldown, an open breaker immediately allows a trial and moves to half-open
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 1, cooldownMs: 0 }); b.recordFailure(); const allowed = b.canAttempt(); return allowed && b.state === "half-open"; })()).toBe(true)

tests.description: a failed trial in half-open reopens the breaker
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 1, cooldownMs: 0 }); b.recordFailure(); b.canAttempt(); b.recordFailure(); return b.state; })()).toBe("open")

tests.description: the breaker does not open before reaching the threshold
tests.expr: expect((() => { const b = new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 5, cooldownMs: 0 }); b.recordFailure(); return b.state; })()).toBe("closed")

items.explanation: Because a failed trial still counts as a failure, recordFailure's existing threshold logic naturally reopens the breaker on a failed half-open trial — no separate half-open-specific logic is needed, since a threshold of 1 (already reached) triggers immediately again.
